paragraphs.source_en: “As for Yagi Dokusen, whom I had admired and had very much intended to take as my model, judging from what Meitei says, he seems not to be a man especially worth imitating after all. Not only that, but the doctrine he advocates somehow departs from common sense and, as Meitei says, appears to belong somewhat to the system of lunacy. Moreover, he plainly has two mad disciples, which makes the matter all the more dangerous. If I carelessly draw near him, I may very well be dragged into that same system. Tendo Kohei, whose writing I admired so extravagantly that I convinced myself he must be a great man of exceptional insight, is in real name that Tachimachi Soba, a pure madman, and is in fact living in the Sugamo asylum. Even if Meitei’s account is an outrageously exaggerated piece of nonsense, it is probably true that in the asylum he enjoys a great reputation and appoints himself ruler of the Heavenly Way. And I, parroting after him like this, may perhaps have a touch of the same thing myself. For like calls to like and birds of a feather flock together; after all, I have admired a madman’s arguments. At the very least, since I have felt sympathy with his style and words, I too must be a close relation of madness. Even if I am not cast and assimilated into their type, should I take up residence next door to a madman, there is no telling that I might not someday knock through the single wall between us and, before I knew it, be sitting knee to knee with him in the same room, laughing and talking. This is a serious danger. When I think it over carefully, indeed, my brain’s workings lately have been so startling even to myself that one might say they have added strangeness upon marvel and oddity upon grotesquerie. Leaving aside the chemical changes in a ladleful of brain fluid, the movement of the will turns into action and at the same time issues forth as speech. Looking back over my recent words and deeds, it is truly strange: there are many points at which I have lost the mean. Even if I do not feel a Dragon Spring sword upon my tongue or a pure breeze rising beneath my arms, what am I to do if there is a mad stench at the roots of my teeth and a flavor of lunacy at the tips of my sinews? This grows more and more alarming; for all I know, I may already be a splendid patient. Fortunately, I have not yet injured anyone or done anything to trouble the world, and so perhaps I have not been driven out by the neighborhood and am still allowed to exist here as a citizen of Tokyo. This is no stage for talk of passive or active; first I must examine my pulse. However, there seems to be nothing unusual in my pulse. Could my head be feverish? That too shows no particular sign of excitement. Still, somehow it leaves me uneasy.”
